Baltic Exchange data cited by Reuters showed the Gulf of Oman-to-China VLCC route at around WS450 on September 11 , equivalent to approximately $11.50 per barrel , the highest level since the assessment was introduced earlier in 2026.
West Africa-to-Asia VLCC rates had also reached record highs as Middle East security risks reduced available tonnage.
The East-West Pipeline outage adds another layer to that dislocation by reducing Saudi Arabia’s ability to shift export flows between the Gulf and the Red Sea.
First, reduced westbound flexibility could force Saudi Arabia to route more crude back through Gulf export terminals and the Hormuz-linked shipping system. Reuters reported that Ras Tanura and Juaymah loaded around 22m barrels on 12 vessels during the week of September 7–13, compared with six or seven vessels in each of the previous three weeks.
That matters because Gulf-to-Asia transport is already exceptionally expensive. Higher dependence on Gulf loading, ship-to-ship transfers and war-risk arrangements raises delivered crude costs even if Saudi barrels remain physically available.
Second, European refiners seeking US, Guyanese, Algerian, North Sea and other alternative grades are competing in some of the same non-Gulf supply pools that Asian refiners can use to diversify away from Middle Eastern risk.
The result is a potential increase in both crude differentials and tonne-mile demand.

While roughly one-fifth of global seaborne oil exports were disrupted, Frontline said the resulting market dislocation actually boosted tanker demand through longer voyages, rerouted cargoes, and widespread inefficiencies.

A single supertanker now costs $1.27 million a day to charter, a record, after Saudi Arabia rerouted crude away from the Red Sea port of Yanbu and jammed up the ship-to-ship transfer trade off Oman.
The diversion, prompted by Houthi attacks on shipping, has pushed transfer capacity in the Gulf of Oman to its ceiling, according to Reuters, which cited unnamed trading sources and analysts. The freight spike is the clearest sign yet that the physical crude market is paying a growing premium simply to move barrels safely.
Buyers are absorbing the cost of longer routes and scarce tanker slots without bidding the headline number sharply higher, at least for now.
Saudi barrels take the long way around
Yanbu sits on the Red Sea, and Red Sea traffic has become a liability. With Houthi strikes making the route dangerous, Saudi flows have shifted, and the crude that would normally load cleanly is instead being handled through ship-to-ship transfers off Oman.
A rising channel that just got rejected
The freight premium the futures screen isn’t showing
For now the split holds: crude flat, freight at an all-time high, equities under pressure, silver steadier, and the euro unusually quiet against the dollar — all of it running through the same barrel of oil. Saudi Arabia has already sold cargoes into the new routing, and the tanker market has repriced accordingly.

Middle Eastern oil exports recover to highest level since Iran war began
28 September 2026 10:01
Crude oil exports from major Middle Eastern producers rebounded to 12.8 million barrels per day in September, reaching their highest level since the war started in February, according to preliminary data from analytics firm Kpler cited by Reuters .
According to Kpler’s estimates, oil exports through the Strait of Hormuz were set to reach around 7.4 million barrels per day in September. Following damage to the East-West pipeline in attacks, Saudi Arabia redirected part of its export flows from the Red Sea port of Yanbu.
Saudi oil exports are approaching 5.4 million barrels per day in September, compared with 2.446 million barrels per day in August. At the same time, shipments from the Ras Tanura port rose to around 3.6 million barrels per day, up from 929,000 barrels per day in August.
According to Kpler, 19 very large crude carriers (VLCCs) passed out of the Strait of Hormuz last week, each carrying around 2 million barrels of Saudi crude.
Despite the recovery in shipments, total oil exports from the region remain around 6 million barrels per day below their February level.
By Jeyhun Aghazada

Oil prices rose despite crude exports from major Middle Eastern producers reaching 12.8 million barrels a day, the highest since the war began, as Saudi Arabian and Emirati shipments increased.
Ship-to-Ship Reliance Keeps Middle East Export Costs Elevated
Higher export volumes overstate the recovery in normal trade flows because much of the increase still relies on ship-to-ship transfers. Tim Waterer, Chief Market Analyst at KCM Trade, says ship-to-ship transfers are less efficient and more costly than normal operations.
What Keeps Brent Above $106
Middle Eastern crude exports reached a wartime high of 12.8 million barrels a day, yet Brent November futures remained at $106.99 a barrel. September's export recovery did not relieve transport or refining constraints, shifting scarcity from crude supply to downstream capacity.
Refining constraints shifted more value toward distillate margins.

candidates.source_name: Five loaded Qatari LNG vessels approach Hormuz
candidates.snippet:
LONDON: Five vessels loaded with liquefied natural gas (LNG) from Ras Laffan, Qatar, are approaching the Strait of Hormuz, ship-tracking data showed on Saturday.
If the vessels successfully crossed the strait, it would be the first transit of LNG cargoes through the waterway since the US-Israel war with Iran began on February 28.
On Friday, Iran reopened the strait, which before the war carried a fifth of the world’s LNG trade, following a separate US-brokered ceasefire agreement on Thursday by Israel and Lebanon. A convoy of oil tankers was crossing the Strait of Hormuz on Saturday.
“Currently we see five laden vessels approaching the Strait of Hormuz. All five vessels loaded from Qatar’s Ras Laffan plant. Of the five, two are destined for Pakistan, two likely destined for India and one with no clear destination,” said Laura Page, manager of LNG Insight at Kpler.
“In addition, two ballast Adnoc vessels enter the Gulf of Oman and moor outside Fujairah. The vessel movements align with flaring data which suggests multiple trains at Ras Laffan’s north site have restarted as well as UAE’s Das Island plant,” she added.
Qatar is the world’s second-largest exporter of LNG, with shipments mostly going to buyers in Asia. Iranian attacks, however, knocked out 17 per cent of Qatar’s LNG export capacity, with repairs expected to sideline 12.8 million metric tonnes per year of the fuel for three to five years.

candidates.snippet:
Firestorm Labs is a San Diego defense company that sells two things at once: cheap additively manufactured drones, and the containerised factory that prints them.
Its argument is that the binding constraint on attritable UAS is not the airframe but the supply line behind it, and that a unit able to make and repair aircraft where it is fighting does not need one. Its customers are US military organisations, across every service branch.
Products
Firestorm says an xCell can turn out drone systems within 24 hours, and the Army has used one to make parts for Bradley Fighting Vehicles — repair parts, not just aircraft, are a large share of the pitch.
Tempest is the modular UAS designed to be produced by xCell, supporting ISR, electronic warfare and kinetic payloads.
Business and Contracts
In May 2026 it was reported to have won a $30 million APFIT award, extendable to $50 million, covering five xCell units, more than 200 Tempest drones and operator training for an undisclosed Indo-Pacific customer.
Magy has said he wants xCell at full operational deployment across the Indo-Pacific within about two years — a stated goal, not a programme of record.
Why It Matters
Firestorm competes on logistics rather than aircraft performance, which is a genuinely different position in a crowded small-UAS market and explains why both Lockheed Martin Ventures and In-Q-Tel are on the cap table. If forward units can print and replace drones without resupply, the economics of attritable systems change.

candidates.source_name: The 2025 National Defense Authorization Act: What’s Actually Changing in the Military — Enstartup
candidates.snippet:
Tech, Drones, and the "Replicator" Initiative
If you follow defense tech, you know the Ukraine conflict changed everything. We saw that expensive, multi-million dollar platforms can be taken out by a $500 drone from a hobby shop. The 2025 National Defense Authorization Act reflects this shift.
It puts a heavy emphasis on "attritable" systems—basically, gear that is cheap enough to lose in combat without breaking the bank.
👉 See also: The Door That Only Opens One Way
The Pentagon’s "Replicator" initiative gets a serious nod here.
The goal is to field thousands of small, smart, autonomous systems across multiple domains within the next 18 to 24 months. Think swarms of drones in the air and unmanned boats in the water. This isn't just sci-fi anymore. The bill allocates billions specifically for the Indo-Pacific region to deter potential conflict in the Taiwan Strait.
If you’re a defense contractor working on AI or autonomous sensors, your 2025 is looking very busy.
At the end of the day, the 2025 National Defense Authorization Act is a reflection of a world that feels increasingly dangerous. It moves the needle on troop pay, doubles down on drone technology, and tries to fix a broken procurement system that takes too long to get gear into the hands of soldiers.
Is it perfect? Not even close.
It’s a 3,000-page compromise. But it sets the stage for a military that is smaller, tech-heavier, and hopefully, better compensated.

The US Army selected five companies on August 26 to build nuclear microreactors at five installations. The agreements are worth up to $2.2 billion through fiscal 2031. The program is called Janus.
Fuel choices differ across the group. Radiant and Antares plan to use HALEU in TRISO form. General Atomics plans uranium zirconium hydride. Jeff Waksman, the Principal Deputy Assistant Secretary of the Army for Installations, Energy and Environment, leads the effort on the Army side.
The Army frames Janus as energy independence.
A 1 MW to 20 MW generator that runs for years without refueling is a microgrid asset, not a power plant. Diesel gensets and batteries carry most installations through an outage today. Both depend on fuel deliveries or on a short discharge window. A reactor sized to a base changes the resilience math, because the fuel is already on site.
They do not speed up the licensing.
Milestone-based payment protects the money, not the timeline. If Antares, BWXT, General Atomics, Radiant and Westinghouse all slip together, the Army has spent little and gained nothing on schedule. The resilience claim needs a test as well.

The two types of DOD bases face the same challenge, but for different reasons. In Afghanistan, the diesel generators that provide electricity at bases are the top consumer of fuel on the battlefield.
One way to reduce that fuel use is to generate more power on site, through distributed generation technologies like solar or waste-to-power plants. Another is to use that power more efficiently. And another is to network the base’s power sources and loads together into a microgrid that can be managed intelligently.
Anyway, that’s the battlefield microgrid stuff, and it’s really cool. But I want to focus on the state-side “stationary” bases. If successful, even a total blackout of the larger grid would not affect power on the base. And though the primary purpose is security-related, it would also help DOD meet its clean-energy goals.

Today, the European Commission has approved an additional €6.1 billion for Ukraine to procure different defence products in the field of air and missile defence , ammunition , drones and electronic warfare .
This essential funding will support Ukraine's capacity to withstand the continued intensification of Russian ballistic missile and drone strikes.
Ursula von der Leyen , President of the European Commission: “Today, we have approved €6.1 billion to help Ukraine procure different defence products in the field of air and missile defence, ammunition, drones and electronic warfare.
With this approval, Ukraine can now also purchase the Patriot equipment it needs to better protect its skies from Russia's indiscriminate attacks. Together with our Member States and NATO, we will continue to deliver for Ukraine while strengthening Europe's own defence.”
These funds will support the procurement of defence products from both EU and Ukrainian companies. Following agreement by EU Member States on Monday, the decision also enables Ukraine to procure PAC-3 missiles for Patriot systems.
Funded under the €90 billion Ukraine Support Loan, the package includes five derogations from standard eligibility conditions: three for Ukrainian-made drones and components exceeding cost thresholds, and two for US-made equipment, in particular PAC-3 missiles, including via the NATO-coordinated PURL mechanism.
